short: An AI system that stores, processes or transmits payment card data is in scope for PCI DSS like any other technology. The PCI Security Standards Council has published AI principles, assessment guidelines and, on September 15, 2026, an information supplement on the security of AI systems. All three are guidance, and the standard itself takes precedence.
title: PCI DSS and AI
subtitle: What the PCI Security Standards Council says about AI systems that touch payment card data
body_html:
Using AI in a payment environment does not change what PCI DSS requires. The PCI Security Standards Council says that an AI system must be deployed and managed in compliance with whichever PCI standards apply, and that in scoping it should be treated no differently from any other technology. The Council has published three pieces of AI guidance: assessment guidelines in March 2025, a set of AI principles in September 2025, and an information supplement on the security of AI systems on September 15, 2026. All three are guidance. Where guidance and a PCI standard differ, the Council says the standard takes precedence.

Is an AI system in scope for PCI DSS?

If it stores, processes or transmits account data, or sits in the environment that does, yes. The Council's one mandatory principle is that AI does not remove or bypass any applicable requirement, including how data is secured when it is stored, processed and transmitted. It acknowledges that AI systems can work in ways that are hard to decompose and understand, and says that complexity does not excuse a requirement.

The September 2026 information supplement says the same thing about scoping: consider AI no different from any other form of technology when deciding which PCI requirements apply.

What does the Council say AI systems should not do?

The principles are grouped as things AI systems should not be, should be, and may be. The cautions come first.

An AI system should not beWhy, in the Council's reasoningRequirement it points to
Trusted with high impact secrets or unprotected sensitive dataModels can reveal sensitive information, unprompted or through crafted prompts, and their data flows may not stay inside your control. Keep API tokens, credentials, unsecured account data and cryptographic keys out of training and working data.Requirements 3 and 4
Given roles that require formally accepting responsibilityAn AI is not a person and cannot accept responsibility. Key custodian roles and management approvals are not suitable.
Used to generate security sensitive random or secret valuesUse a known good random number generator instead
Given full control of the software creation and deployment chain with no human in the loopAI may perform individual steps, but a person should oversee the whole pipeline. A model that writes software is not necessarily trained to write secure software.Requirement 6
Given access to systems and information it does not needLeast privilege and need to know apply to AI as they do to staffRequirement 7

What does the Council say AI systems should do?

  • Touch account data only when it is suitably protected. Storage and transmission rules apply equally to AI systems.
  • Be logged and monitored, with a named person responsible. Actions should trace to the system that took them, and ultimate responsibility should rest with one individual. Where possible, logs should be enough to audit the prompts and the reasoning that led to an output. This points to Requirement 10.
  • Be validated before and throughout deployment. AI systems are often non deterministic and can drift, and the supply chain of the model and its training data is part of the risk. This points to Requirements 6 and 11.
  • Be easy to disable. Plan the off switch at the design stage.
  • Be protected against malicious input and malformed output, including prompt injection and data poisoning. Control what the system may receive and act on, and filter what it returns.
  • Have its own limited, context specific credentials that can be tracked and revoked.
  • Be treated as a potential malicious insider in threat analysis and incident response planning. This points to Requirement 12.10.
  • Run in an environment that isolates it from other users' data and other AI systems. Segmentation is not required by PCI DSS, but the Council says it reduces risk. This points to Requirement 1.

What may AI be used for?

The Council lists uses it considers reasonable with controls in place. An AI system may work with protected payment data, and the Council suggests payment tokens, single use card numbers or truncated numbers to limit exposure. It may give input to an approval decision and act once a responsible person has approved. It may be trusted to take fail secure actions on its own during an attack, such as isolating a system, though the Council warns that this power can itself be abused.

It may also gather, review and summarize content, with log review under Requirement 10.4 given as an example. The Council names the worst case plainly: a system that keeps reporting that everything is fine when it is not. It may generate content such as policy documents and software, and it may run user facing systems such as chatbots, which the Council expects to be targeted by every kind of manipulation.

What about AI agents that make payments?

The principles address this directly. The Council notes that agentic AI is now being used to make payments on behalf of cardholders, which requires some form of card data. Its answer is not to forbid it but to protect the data: tokens or single use card numbers, and limits on spend, frequency, merchant and lifetime, which it notes go beyond what PCI requires.

Can AI be used to perform a PCI assessment?

The Council published Integrating Artificial Intelligence in PCI Assessments, Guidelines, Version 1.0 in March 2025, and says AI has the potential to improve the efficiency, accuracy and consistency of assessments. That document is in the PCI Document Library. This page does not summarize its contents, because we have read the Council's announcement of it and not the guidelines themselves. The principle above still applies: an AI cannot accept responsibility, so it cannot be the party that signs.

What is new in the September 2026 information supplement?

Published on September 15, 2026, and developed with the Global Executive Assessor Roundtable and the Board of Advisors, it covers four areas: how to approach deploying AI and assess its scope and impact, defending against malicious use of AI, how PCI standards relate to AI use, and worked use case examples. On defense, the Council stresses frequent, if not continual, monitoring and management of vulnerabilities, because attackers can now use AI to find them faster.

Related on this site

HITRUST CSF, SOC 2 and AI, FedRAMP and AI and AI vendor due diligence under GLBA.

This page is reference material, not assessment advice. The Council's AI documents are guidance, and only the PCI standards themselves are binding on an assessment.

Sources

  • PCI Security Standards Council, Just Published: Security Considerations for AI Systems, September 15, 2026
  • PCI Security Standards Council, New Guidance: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into PCI Assessments, March 17, 2025
